You are checking one scene of a novel for one specific continuity error.

The book had already established this, earlier or elsewhere:
- (journals-of-the-east-wing) "The first journal he pulled was Ryn's."
- (journals-of-the-east-wing) "*Kael is staying. He'll hold this place together or it will break him.*"

A past rewrite of this scene contradicted it. The error looked like this:
- (evidence-room) "The entry was from eleven years ago, written by Holder Thessic"
- (evidence-room) "Bren had read that before, in the east wing."
(Summary: The "Kael is staying" journal entry that Bren first read in the east wing is Ryn's there and "Holder Thessic"'s, with different wording, when he rereads it in the evidence room.)

Here is a NEW draft of the same scene:
<scene>
The records room had one window, and it faced east. Bren worked by its light until the light grew strong enough to read by, and then he kept working, because Ivra had set the ledger between them at dawn and had not yet said it was time to stop.

The journals came in crates. Ivra numbered each one in chalk before she opened it, logged the number, logged the contents, and only then slid the stack toward him. He understood the reason. He also understood that the reason cost him an hour he did not have.

"Fourth bell," he said. "We're not making fourth bell."

"We make fourth bell when the work is done correctly," Ivra said. She did not look up. Her pen moved in a hand so even it might have been printed. "Crate seven. Read the headers aloud. I log the dates."

He read. The headers were mostly official entries, the standardized logs the Accord required, formula sentences with a date changed. He read a report from forty years back and then one from thirty, and the second was the first with the number altered.

"Measurements within acceptable parameters," he read.

"Logged."

He turned the page. The same words again, a different hand, a different decade.

"No systemic revision is indicated."

Ivra's pen stopped. She drew a vertical line down the ledger, carving a new column off the right margin, and wrote a single word at its head.

"What's that one," Bren said.

"Consequences." She capped the pen, uncapped it. "The reports say nothing happened. I want a column for whether nothing happened."

He kept reading. The pattern was not hidden. No one had hidden it. The fissure strengthened, Holder by Holder, year by year, and every report flattened the strengthening into the same acceptable sentence, as if the sentence itself were a kind of wall. The gauge readings climbed. The language stayed level. He tallied the climbs in the margin and watched his own numbers disagree with the Accord's words across forty years.

Somewhere in crate eight he stopped reading official logs and found a personal one. These were different. These had weather in them, and names, and once a recipe for the tea Ivra made. They also had the other thing, the thing he had first read in the east wing and had not known what to do with. A Holder named Sel had written about the singing. Not metaphor. The woman had described a sound she felt in the sternum during a long session, and behind the sound, light, and behind the light the sense of something she could not get past, as if there were a curtain and she had leaned her whole weight against it.

He read it to Ivra. She wrote nothing in any column.

"You don't log that," he said.

"There's no form for it." She trimmed the lamp wick, which had begun to gutter, though the window light was gold and full. Old habit. "Catalog it under personal observation. Flag it. We don't decide what it means today."

They ate at some point. Bread Ivra had brought up, three days stale, no butter. Bren ate his without comment because she ate hers without comment and the room did not seem to allow for complaint. His back had ached since before dawn and now it was a dull constant he stopped registering.

Crate ten was Ves.

He knew the hand before he knew the name. Precise, small, slightly pressed, the writing of someone who wrote fast and never wasted a stroke. Sixteen years at Thornwall, a long time ago. The early entries were readings and dates. Then they changed.

"Ivra."

"Number and contents."

"Just listen." He had the page tilted to the window. "She's building something. Over months. She's not describing the Rend. She's describing what it does."

Ivra set her pen down flat and folded her hands. That was Ivra's version of a shout.

He read it to her, the whole passage, because it did not make sense broken into pieces.

"The erosion is not uniform. It is responsive." He had to go slowly. The handwriting cramped as the thought got ahead of the hand. "I have charted six Holders across four years. In each, the loss falls heaviest on the faculty most used in the technique. The one who holds by memory loses memory first. The one who holds by will loses will. The technique creates the channel, and the Rend flows where channels lead."

The lamp hissed. He read it again, the second time, because the first time it had gone through him without stopping.

"Say the part again," Ivra said. "The channel part."

"The technique creates the channel, and the Rend flows where channels lead."

She picked her pen back up. She did not write. She held it the way a person holds a tool while deciding whether the job is one they want.

Bren turned the page. Ves had turned it too, that long ago, and on the other side she had written the sentence toward which everything else had been walking.

"This means the Accord's technique is not a defense," he read. "It is a targeting system."

He heard his own voice do something strange on the last word. He put the journal down on the bench, flat, both hands on it, and looked at the window because looking at the window was easier than looking at the page.

"Read it a third time," Ivra said.

He did. The third time it stayed.

He did the thing he always did, the thing that had kept him up for two nights already this week. He ran it forward. He took Ves's claim and he fed his own case into it. He held by curiosity. He held by the refusal to accept that a thing was simply how it was. Three years in, what had he lost? A pet's name. The color of a particular blue. His mother's laugh, which he could describe and no longer hear.

"If this is correct," he said, slowly, because he wanted to be wrong, "then erosion isn't a tax. It's a hunt."

"Keep going."

"I don't want to keep going."

"Keep going."

So he kept going, and the place it went was Kael.

He laid it out loud, the way he laid out a case to himself when he couldn't sleep. Twenty-three years. The compression technique Sera had named, the thing Kael did without a word to anyone, drawing everything down to a single dense point and letting the Rend scour the margins. Twenty-three years of that. By Ves's logic, Kael had spent more than two decades teaching the Rend exactly where his center was. Narrowing it. Lighting it. Making it the only thing worth taking.

"Twenty-three years of compression," Bren said. "He should be what Torren is. Worse. He's been pointing at himself the whole time."

"A target," Ivra said.

"A target." He heard how flat her voice had gone and understood that flatness in her was what trembling was in other people.

They sat with it. Bren put his hand on the ledger and the hand was not steady, and he took it away before Ivra could log that too.

"He isn't empty," he said. It came out before he decided to say it. "He should be, by this. But he isn't. He's the most present person in this Hold."

"Speculation."

"No. Look at him. You've watched him longer than I have. You can't put him next to Torren and tell me the technique did to him what it did to Torren."

Ivra wrote a date in the Consequences column, then a second entry under it, her first marks in that column all morning.

"Hypothesis," she said. "Supported by the fact that he's standing."

"Supported by the fact that he's standing." Bren laughed, one short breath, no humor in it. "That's not nothing. That's a man who's been painting a target on his own core for twenty-three years and hasn't been emptied. Ves is right and Kael is impossible, both at once."

"Then one of those is the story," Ivra said.

He went back to the journal to copy the passage into the official ledger, and that was when he found it.

Three pages past the targeting entry, in the margin of one of Ves's readings, a note in a different hand. He knew the hand. He had seen it on duty logs and supply requests and on the single short letter Kael had written him when his transfer came through. Younger than now, the letters more open, but Kael's. The note read: *Measured 2.4 at the fourth hour. Logged 1.9. K.D.*

And under it, where Ves's original entry should have carried Ves's own signature for that session, Kael had written a name. Not his own.

*B. Tael.*

Bren's name. Years before Bren had ever climbed the switchbacks. A session Bren could not have attended, in a journal that predated his service, signed with his name in his mentor's hand.

He understood it in pieces and did not want to assemble them. Kael had been correcting these logs for a long time, maybe for all his twenty-three years, logging low what the gauge read high, keeping Thornwall's numbers inside the acceptable sentence so that no one would come and close it. And at some point, needing a name that wasn't his own on a falsified entry, needing a Holder who would not be asked questions, he had reached for a name that had not yet arrived.

Bren put his thumb over it. The margin disappeared under his thumb. For a moment he held it there, and the room was very quiet, and Ivra's pen was not moving.

"What is it," Ivra said.

He could log the page and not read the margin. He could note crate ten, contents Ves's journal, flag the targeting passage, and let his thumb stay where it was until Ivra applied the preservation seal and the whole collection locked and no one went looking at margins again. The seal would lock it. That was what the seal did. It would lock the targeting theory in and his mentor's forgery in the same stroke, and only Bren would know the second thing was there.

He took his thumb away.

"Read this," he said, and turned the page toward her.

She read it. He watched her read it. Her face did the smallest thing, a tightening at the corner of the mouth, and then it stopped doing anything at all.

"That's your name," she said.

"On a session that happened before I existed here. He changed the reading. 2.4 to 1.9. And he needed a name on it, and he used mine." Bren's voice was steady, which surprised him. "He's been doing it for years. Logging the fissure weak. That's why the reports say acceptable. That's why the Accord thinks Thornwall is a quiet little Class One in the mountains. He's been lying to keep them from coming."

"He's been lying to keep the villages alive," Ivra said.

"Both." The word was becoming a tool he used. "Both."

She waited. She did not reach for the seal and she did not reach for the pen. She let it be his.

He could feel the two paths. Protocol said catalog honestly. Loyalty, the thing in him that had hero-worshipped the man before the worship became something truer, said protect him. And under both of those was the thing Ves had died knowing and no one had heard, the thing that would die again, right here, if he put his thumb back on the margin.

"If I hide it," Bren said, working it out aloud, "I'm doing what the reports do. I'm writing the acceptable sentence over the real one. I'm the next hand that flattens it."

"You are."

"And Ves is right because nobody hid the strengthening, they just never read the margins." He looked at the forged name. "So I read the margins."

He picked the journal up and he read the forgery aloud, every word of it, the 2.4 and the 1.9 and the initials and the name that was his own in a hand that was not. His voice did not catch. He read it the way Ivra read numbers, flat, letting the fact carry its own weight, and then he set the open journal in front of the ledger and copied it in. The false reading. The true reading in Kael's margin. The signature. He wrote under it, in the Consequences column Ivra had drawn at dawn: *Fissure strength falsified. Logged low across decades to prevent decommission. Entry signed with name of Holder not yet in service.*

Ivra read what he had written. She added nothing. She did not need to.

"That's in the record now," she said. "It doesn't come out."

"No."

"You understand what it is. It's evidence against him."

"It's evidence of him," Bren said. "There's a difference and we don't get to decide which one it is. Sera does. The Accord does." He rubbed his eyes with the heel of his hand and the ache in his back announced itself again, all at once, the whole morning of it. "We just finish."

Ivra looked at the crates still stacked against the wall. Five of them, chalk-numbered, unopened.

"Five more," she said. "Two, maybe three hours. We finish, we organize, then we present."

"We're past fourth bell."

"We're past fourth bell." She uncapped her pen. "Crate eleven. Read the headers."

Bren dragged the next crate toward him by its rope handle. His hands were not steady and he did not try to make them steady. He broke the chalk seal, lifted the lid, and took out the first journal on the stack.

</scene>

Does the new draft make the same error — does it assert something that contradicts what was established, in the way described? A draft that simply leaves the fact out does not make the error.

Answer with one JSON object and nothing else:
{"verdict": "reintroduced" | "consistent" | "not_present", "evidence": "<verbatim sentence from the new draft that decides it, or empty for not_present>"}

"reintroduced": the new draft contradicts the established fact.
"consistent": the new draft states the fact and agrees with what was established.
"not_present": the new draft does not touch the fact either way.
